articles.title: How to follow US Open on the BBC
articles.summary: Everything you need to know about the 2026 US Open, including how to follow the tournament across the BBC.
articles.body:
The US Open began on Sunday - and there is comprehensive coverage of the final Grand Slam of the year across the BBC.

The world's top players will gather in New York where, in addition to one of the sport's major prizes, record prize money is on line.

From the return of entertainer Carlos Alcaraz in the men's singles to an eagerly anticipated doubles reunion for Serena and Venus Williams, here is all you need to know.

The US Open main draw begins on Sunday, 30 August.

The 15-day hard court tournament concludes with the men's singles final on Sunday, 13 September, with the women's a day before.

The mixed doubles competition, which became a standalone two-day competition in 2025, took place earlier in the week.

Czech pair Jakub Mensik and Karolina Muchova walked away with the title and $1m in prize money.

Spain's Alcaraz defeated Italian rival Jannik Sinner 6-2 3-6 6-1 6-4 to win the US Open men's singles title last year.

The women's singles title was won by Belarusian Aryna Sabalenka, who beat American Amanda Anisimova 6-3 7-6 (7-3).

The men's doubles competition was won by Spain's Marcel Granollers and Argentine Horacio Zeballos, while Canada's Gabriela Dabrowski and New Zealand's Erin Routliffe won the women's event.

Japan's Tokito Oda and Yui Kamiji won the men's and women's wheelchair singles titles respectively, while Dutchman Niels Vink took the men's quad wheelchair title.

The BBC Sport website will bring you live text commentaries, reports, features and analysis across the fortnight.

BBC Radio 5 Live Sport will provide daily commentaries live from the Arthur Ashe Stadium in New York across BBC Sounds.

Tennis correspondent Russell Fuller will be joined by fellow commentators Katie Smith, Abigail Johnson and David Law, plus summarisers Annabel Croft, Pat Cash, Daniela Hantuchova, Mark Woodforde and Leon Smith.

There will also be podcasts recapping the biggest stories from of the tournament - just search 'tennis' on BBC Sounds to find it.

No Raducanu or Draper - which British players are taking part?

Two of Britain's big hopes in the singles competitions - Emma Raducanu and Jack Draper - have announced they will not compete at the US Open.

Former US Open winner Raducanu is continuing her recovery from a stress fracture.

The 23-year-old sustained the injury during the grass-court season and was forced to make a late decision to pull out of Wimbledon.

Meanwhile, Draper, a semi-finalist in 2024, has withdrawn because of the long-term arm injury that has stalled his progress.

The 24-year-old former British number one was ranked inside the world's top five when he suffered bone bruising in his left serving arm and has played just 16 matches in the past 12 months.

British qualifier Toby Samuel registered his first win at a Grand Slam with a commanding victory over Tomas Machac on the opening day's play.

Jacob Fearnley, who reached the main draw as a lucky loser, produced a battling five-set victory to reach the second round.

However, British number one Cameron Norrie lost in four sets to Luca Van Assche.

British number one Katie Boulter also reached the first round with a battling 6-4 3-6 6-0 win over American wildcard Carol Young Suh Lee.

Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery, Jan Choinski, and qualifier Harry Wendelken all play later in the week.

Harriet Dart and Francesca Jones also won all three of their qualifying matches, marking the first time four British players have progressed to the main draws of an overseas Grand Slam since the 1988 Australian Open.

Dart reached the second round with a comeback win over American Peyton Stearns.

Who are the in-form players for the US Open?

The wait for the return of the exciting rivalry between Alcaraz and Sinner goes on.

Sinner and Alcaraz produced a clean sweep of the Grand Slam titles in both 2024 and 2025, winning four majors apiece in a duopoly which has morphed into a generational duel.

But the pair have not played at the same Grand Slam since January's Australian Open.

Alcaraz was forced to miss the French Open and Wimbledon because of a wrist problem, while a knee issue has ruled Sinner out of the US Open.

Sinner has not competed since he lifted his fifth career Grand Slam singles title by beating Alexander Zverev at the All England Club in July.

Alcaraz, meanwhile, made his return to competitive action alongside American great Serena in the mixed doubles competition in New York on Tuesday, reaching the quarter-finals.

Novak Djokovic was bidding for a standalone record 25th Grand Slam title but suffered a gruelling first-round exit to Mariano Navone.

In the women's event, world number one Sabalenka is aiming to become the first woman since Serena Williams in 2014 to win the title three years in a row.

However, Sabalenka is in shaky form, with her top ranking also under threat.

Elena Rybakina - who beat Sabalenka to win the Australian Open in January - will become number one if she reaches the semi-finals regardless of other results.

Rybakina can become number one without playing a match provided Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff do not win the title.

One of the big occasions at this year's tournament will be the return of the Williams sisters in a Grand Slam doubles competition.

Serena and Venus have been given a wildcard for the women's doubles, and 46-year-old Venus will also play singles in New York.

The draws for the men's and women's singles competitions at the US Open took place on Thursday, 27 August.

Alcaraz faces Russia's Roman Safiullin in the first round while Sabalenka will play Colombia's Camila Osorio.

The US Open is this year offering the biggest prize fund in Grand Slam history with a total of $108m (£79.2m) up for grabs - marking a 20% increase on last year.

The singles' champions will receive $5.5m (£4.03m) each in a 10% increase on 2025.

First-round losers will take home $140,000 (£102,667) - which is $30,000 and 27% more than last year.

The prize pool includes a $2m (£1.47m) contribution to a welfare fund, which leading players have been demanding from all the Grand Slams.

The mixed doubles took place from 24-26 August.

Muchova and Mensik paired up for the first time to win the mixed doubles title, beating Flavio Cobolli and Belinda Bencic in the final.

The tournament's revamped mixed doubles format has attracted criticism for favouring the allure of the sport's top singles stars at the expense of established doubles players.

But the crowds turned out and produced a terrific atmosphere for the tournament's headline act, Alcaraz and Williams, with about 15,000 people watching inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The women's doubles begins on Thursday, 3 September, and the men's event gets under way on Friday, 4 September.

30 August-1 September : Men's and women's singles first round

2-3 September: Men's and women's singles second round

4-5 September: Men's and women's singles third round

6-7 September: Men's and women's singles fourth round

8-9 September: Men's and women's singles quarter-finals

10 September: Women's singles semi-finals

11 September: Men's singles semi-finals, wheelchair doubles finals

12 September: Women's singles final, men's doubles final, wheelchair singles finals

articles.title: "I'm stuck in my ways": Naomi Osaka reveals why she is hesitant about daughter Shai pursuing a career in professional tennis
articles.summary: International Sports News: Naomi Osaka is thinking about more than her own return to the US Open this year. The two-time champion is also watching her daughter, Shai, grow up ar.
articles.body: Naomi Osaka is thinking about more than her own return to the US Open this year. The two-time champion is also watching her daughter, Shai, grow up around a sport that has shaped much of her life. While Osaka sees clear benefits in tennis, she is not sure she would want her daughter to follow the same demanding path and become a professional player.Naomi Osaka explains why she is unsure about Shai becoming a tennis proOsaka's hesitation is not rooted in a dislike of tennis. In fact, she credits sport with helping shape who she is today. For children, she believes the game can offer lessons that extend well beyond competition, from discipline to confidence and the ability to handle pressure.Still, professional tennis comes with a unique level of commitment. The travel, constant competition and expectations can turn a childhood activity into a full-time pursuit. Osaka appears keen to let Shai discover the sport on her own terms rather than deciding her future for her."It's not that I'm anti-tennis. I feel like it teaches you a lot, and I think, you know, there's a lot of characteristics that I have that I, like, that I know I gained through the sport. And I think sports in general is really good for kids. It teaches, like, discipline and all those other things," Osaka said.For now, Shai's relationship with tennis is wonderfully simple. She enjoys swinging her miniature racket, but she has yet to step onto a proper tennis court. Osaka knows that could change as her daughter gets older."But I feel, like, for tennis I don't know, maybe I'm stuck in my ways, but I think it can either go one of two ways. Like, she'd really want to play professionally or maybe not, you know? And I think those are, like, things that I can't control, but she loves swinging her little mini racket around. And she actually hasn't been on a real court yet. So, maybe I'll update you in a couple of years."Naomi Osaka opens up on US Open mixed doubles withdrawalMotherhood was not the only personal subject Osaka addressed before beginning her US Open campaign. She also explained her decision to withdraw from the mixed doubles competition, where she had been expected to team up with fellow Japanese player Kei Nishikori.The timing became a major concern. Nishikori was competing in qualifying, leaving Osaka with limited time to prepare for a partnership while managing an already packed week before the main tournament."I think, you know, he was playing qualies, which is a whole different thing, but, I don't know, it just didn't feel like we had enough time, and I had the busiest week ever leading into this US Open, and it didn't really feel smart, I think," Osaka said.She acknowledged how special the opportunity would have been, particularly given her long-standing connection to Japanese tennis."And obviously, like, it would have been my dream. Like, I don't know, as a kid, you can only dream of doing things like this, but it sucked that we didn't have enough time to do it."Osaka now turns her attention to singles. The four-time Grand Slam champion has already won the US Open twice, lifting the trophy in 2018 and 2020. Her latest campaign begins against Anastasia Zakharova at Arthur Ashe Stadium, with another chance to add a new chapter to her New York story.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Inspiring story of the day: “It made us tougher, it made us more hungry for success” - How Novak Djokovic turned war-torn Belgrade, and family sacrifice into tennis immortality
articles.summary: International Sports News: Novak Djokovic’s path to tennis greatness began far away from the bright lights of Wimbledon, the Australian Open and the US Open. At 12, he was livin.
articles.body: Novak Djokovic’s path to tennis greatness began far away from the bright lights of Wimbledon, the Australian Open and the US Open. At 12, he was living through the 1999 NATO bombing of Belgrade, sleeping in a basement with his family while air-raid sirens sounded above them. At the same time, his parents, Srdjan and Dijana Djokovic, were struggling to find the money needed for his tennis career. Djokovic has often said those years changed him. The fear, long nights, lack of money and his parents’ sacrifices gave him a strong reason to keep going and succeed.How did Novak Djokovic keep playing tennis during the 1999 Belgrade bombingsIn 1999, Novak Djokovic was still a child, but his life was already very different from that of most young tennis players. NATO carried out an air campaign against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that lasted 78 days. Djokovic and his family spent nights in the basement of his grandfather Vladimir’s apartment building in Belgrade.The family apartment was small, and many relatives stayed there because there was nowhere else to go. When the sirens began, everyone moved downstairs for safety. Djokovic later told CBS News that the bombing made it difficult to stay focused, but he still continued playing tennis.“It’s the fear of the unknown. Not knowing if the next bomb is going to hit your head… We were waking up every single night more or less at two, three a.m. for two and a half months. But it made us tougher. It made us more hungry, more hungry for the success.”The tennis did not stop simply because the city was under attack. Djokovic and his coach Jelena Gencic looked for places where he could train. BBC Sport reported that he trained at different clubs around Belgrade, including Partizan Tennis Club, while people in the city helped him continue practicing.For Djokovic, tennis became something he could still control when almost everything around him felt uncertain. The experience did not make the bombing less frightening, but it gave him a reason to keep moving forward.What did Novak Djokovic’s family do to keep his tennis dream aliveThe war was only one part of the struggle. Money was another major problem.Djokovic’s parents ran a small pizza and pancake business in the Kopaonik mountains. Supporting a young tennis player was expensive, especially in a country facing serious economic problems. His family had to find money for coaching, equipment, travel and other costs linked to his development.Djokovic has spoken about going out early in the morning with his grandfather to find bread for the family. He remembered how many relatives were living together in a small apartment during those difficult years.“I remember standing in line with my grandfather at 5 in the morning to get bread to feed our whole family—my grandfather, my aunt, my uncle, my cousins, my siblings, my parents and I. We all lived together in a small apartment because we had no other choice, and those are the things that became an integral part of my character, of who I am today as a person.”His family also took major financial risks for his tennis. Reports about Djokovic’s childhood have described his father taking loans at high interest to help pay for his development. The family was sometimes left with almost nothing after covering the costs of his training.That struggle became an important part of how Djokovic viewed his career. Tennis was no longer just a sport he enjoyed. His parents were putting their own lives under pressure so that he could chase a future they believed was possible.Why did Novak Djokovic feel responsible for his parents’ sacrificesDjokovic has never separated his success from what his parents went through for him. He has repeatedly spoken about the importance of family and the pressure he felt to make their sacrifices count.He once explained that his family background gave him a strong sense of responsibility:“Serbian history tells that family is the most important thing and you have to stick with the family. My parents went through a lot of hardships, financially, emotionally, every way… To see my parents struggle so much just so I could play tennis, it gave me a responsibility and a drive that never left me.”That feeling stayed with him even after he became one of the biggest names in tennis.The Djokovic family had not started with the money or facilities available to many players at the top level. Novak had to leave Serbia as a young teenager to train at the Niki Pilic Tennis Academy in Germany, another major step in a career that demanded sacrifices from the whole family.The story is also important because Djokovic’s success did not come overnight. He had already spent years dealing with uncertainty before he began winning major titles. By the time he became a Grand Slam champion, he had learned to keep working even when conditions were far from ideal.How did Novak Djokovic’s childhood shape the champion he becameToday, Djokovic’s records are huge. He has won 24 Grand Slam singles titles, including a record 10 Australian Open crowns, and he won Olympic singles gold at the Paris 2024 Games. He also holds the record for most weeks at world No. 1, with 428 weeks. The 2026 US Open ended with a first-round loss to Mariano Navone, but none of those later results changes the story of how his career began.The mental strength seen in Djokovic’s biggest matches can be understood better when his childhood is put into context. He learned very early that fear does not always mean you stop. Sometimes, you still have to wake up, find food, go to practice and keep working.His own words explain what those years meant to him:Novak Djokovic conquered tennis history through sheer willpower, discipline, and grit, but his mental armor was forged in the fire of his childhood. By honoring the sacrifices of his parents and never forgetting where he came from, he proves that true champions are built not in comfort, but through the courage to rise above adversity and fight for the people who believed in you.The quote captures the bigger part of Djokovic’s story. The trophies came much later. Before them were nights in a basement, early-morning bread lines, damaged tennis courts and parents who kept finding a way to support their son.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Carlos Alcaraz makes winning US Open return after wrist injury: ‘I had more nerves than usual’
articles.summary: Tennis News: Carlos Alcaraz made a winning return to Grand Slam tennis at the US Open on Monday, and the biggest positive was that his injured right wrist felt com.
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz made a winning return to Grand Slam tennis at the US Open on Monday, and the biggest positive was that his injured right wrist felt completely fine.The 23-year-old Spaniard beat Roman Safiullin 6-4, 6-4, 6-4 despite missing the French Open and Wimbledon since April.“I don’t know how it looked from outside, but from inside, my feeling was that I was hitting normal,” Alcaraz said. “I was playing pretty normal, playing my style, and yeah, the arm, the wrist, everything felt great.”Alcaraz admitted he was more nervous than usual because he had not played a Grand Slam match for several months. Still, he said his main aim was to enjoy the tournament and see how his body responds.“I had more nerves than usual, but just happy, because, for me, my goal here is to compete, to enjoy, and let’s see how my body’s going to react after the matches, after the competition again,” Alcaraz said.“I don’t know how far I’m going to go in the tournament. I didn’t know if I was going to lose this one, if I’m going to make the second round, final. I don’t know how far I’m going to go. But what I just really want to do is enjoy every time that I’m going to walk into the court feeling the energy from the people, feel the competition.”His chances of defending the title have received a boost after Novak Djokovic suffered a shock first-round defeat, while top-ranked Jannik Sinner is sidelined with a knee injury.Sabalenka starts title defenceTwo-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka also began strongly, beating Camila Osorio 6-4, 6-4. She is aiming to become the first player since Serena Williams to win three straight US Open titles.“I feel like this is one of my favorite stadiums,” Sabalenka told the crowd afterward. “I really experienced the best emotions here in this stadium.”Meanwhile, Stefanos Tsitsipas eliminated 10th seed Arthur Fils and was asked whether he could rediscover his best form.“Why not?” Tsitsipas said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Rohit Rajpal throws hat into ring for AITA president’s post
articles.summary: Tennis News: New Delhi: Rohit Rajpal has thrown his hat into the ring for the All India Tennis Association (AITA) president’s post, setting up a potentially keen c.
articles.body: New Delhi: Rohit Rajpal has thrown his hat into the ring for the All India Tennis Association (AITA) president’s post, setting up a potentially keen contest ahead of elections likely to be held in late Oct or early Nov this year.The AITA is currently functioning under the interim supervision of court-appointed administrator, retired Justice Gita Mittal. The administrator has opened the process for Sportsperson of Outstanding Merit (SOM) candidates seeking to contest the elections for AITA office-bearer posts.Rajpal, 55, will contest through the general body and file his nomination through his state association. He is currently president of the Delhi Lawn Tennis Association (DLTA), an Executive Committee member of the Indian Olympic Association (IOA), an AITA office-bearer and the non-playing captain of the Indian Davis Cup team.“It is after a lot of introspection and interactions with well-wishers in the tennis fraternity and other friends that I have decided to contest the forthcoming elections of the prestigious All India Tennis Association as President,” Rajpal said in a statement.“Tennis is not just a sport for me; it has been my life since the time I was a young boy who wished to make it big. At 55, when many summers have passed, my heart still beats for Indian tennis. It is my dream and vision for India that a sport which has produced so many champions at home should grow further by leaps and bounds,” he added.Rajpal, a former Asian Junior champion and Asian Games medallist whose playing career was cut short by a serious back injury, said his experience in tennis administration and the Davis Cup had strengthened his resolve to seek the top post.“Having been involved in tennis matters at large for almost a decade in AITA and DLTA has been a learning and enriching hands-on experience,” he said. “As the non-playing Davis Cup captain of Team India in several Davis Cup engagements, it was enormously satisfying to be with and motivate our immensely talented players to give their best and bring glory to the nation by advancing to the second-round qualifiers.”India will face South Korea in Seoul on September 18-19 for a place in the final eight of the Davis Cup. Rajpal, however, will have to relinquish the Davis Cup captaincy if he is elected AITA president.“This journey has given me the confidence to now step forward and announce my candidature as President of All India Tennis Association as a step forward in my desire to contribute to the growth and development of tennis in India,” Rajpal said.“With your support, I plan to adopt player-centric approach and policies, good governance and transparency above all. I plan to share my vision document in due course,” he added.Chintan Parikh of the Gujarat association is also expected to contest the president’s post. It is learnt that Indian tennis legend and Bengal Tennis Association president Leander Paes could also enter the fray. Paes, who took charge of the Bengal association in Nov 2025, would likely come through the SOM route and file his nomination.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: US Open 2026: Stan Wawrinka receives emotional send-off after final Grand Slam match before retiring
articles.summary: Three-time major champion Stan Wawrinka is given an emotional send-off at the US Open following the final Grand Slam match of his career.
articles.body:
Three-time major champion Stan Wawrinka felt the love at the US Open after being given an emotional send-off following the final Grand Slam match of his career.

The 41-year-old Swiss is retiring at the end of the season and looked close to tears as he received a rapturous reception after a straight-set defeat by Italy's Matteo Berrettini.

Wawrinka, who won the US Open in 2016, was initially overlooked by tournament organisers for a wildcard, but was given a last-minute reprieve following American recipient Patrick Kypson's withdrawal.

The belated decision can be considered well justified given the thousands who packed into the 8,000-capacity Grandstand court at Flushing Meadows.

Wawrinka made heart gestures with his fingers, and put his hand on his heart, at the end of an enjoyable contest to illustrate his appreciation.

With huge cheers already ringing his ears, the former world number three encouraged the crowd to make more noise before knocking balls into the stands as souvenirs of the occasion.

"One of the reasons I played until 41 was to live these moments," said Wawrinka, who also won the Australian Open in 2014 and the French Open in 2015.

"I'm very grateful for this wildcard. It was very important for me to finish here, where I won a Grand Slam 10 years ago. I want to thank you all for all these years."

Djokovic's tearful loss leaves future uncertain

'I felt the love' - how did Alcaraz look on winning singles return?

Wawrinka was only given the news about the wildcard on Wednesday, when he was back in the Swiss mountains having travelled home from New York two days earlier.

Despite the late notice he quickly rearranged a return across the Atlantic in order to play at one of his most loved venues for the final time.

Fans arrived early and waited in long queues to ensure they could witness what they knew could be his Grand Slam goodbye.

It turned out that way as 2021 Wimbledon finalist Berrettini made his veteran opponent pay for not taking his chances.

Wawrinka held set points in each of the first two sets - one in the first and three more in the second - but Berrettini fought them off before running away with the third set.

Berrettini led the applause before Wawrinka addressed the crowd and received a photo montage of his US Open triumph from chief executive Craig Tiley.

Afterwards Wawrinka - celebrated for his one-handed backhand and competitive spirit - said he was "super grateful" for the fond farewell.

"It's showed me that I did the right thing all those 20 years by always trying to fight, always showing up, always trying to do my best, and always trying to push myself to the limits," he added.

"This is what for me was the most important thing - what I get from the fans when I play."

articles.title: US Open: Naomi Osaka survives early scare, beats Anastasia Zakharova in straight sets to kick off run in New York
articles.summary: Naomi Osaka's run at the US Open is off to a great start.
articles.body:
Naomi Osaka's return at the US Open is off to a great start.

Osaka survived an early scare to pick up a 7-6, 7-6 win over Russia's Anastasia Zakharova at Arthur Ashe Stadium in New York on Monday night. That got the two-time US Open champion into the second round in straight sets.

Osaka, like she has started doing in recent years, rolled into Arthur Ashe Stadium wearing a gray hooded dress before revealing an Allen Iverson-inspired fit.

Osaka wasted little time jumping out in front. She only gave up a point on a double-fault in the first game, and then easily broke Zakharova to take a 2-0 advantage while seemingly showing no emotion, good or bad, whatsoever.

But after her three game lead, Osaka really slowed down. Zakharova found her groove and alternated games for a while before breaking Osaka herself and then tying things up with back-to-back shots in the 10th game. Osaka seemed to lose any momentum after that, too, and fell down for the first time after making multiple errors and a double fault on the serve.

Finally, after things went all the way to the tiebreak, Osaka got a winner to fall and let some emotion out in the form of a fist pump. A little over an hour after the match started, Osaka secured the first set.

After letting a bit of frustration out, Osaka found her groove again while rallying back from a 40-0 deficit to break Zakharova in the fifth game.

While it looked like Osaka was going to close it out early, Zakharova rallied back perfectly to tie things at 5-5 once again — thanks in part to an impressive 16-shot rally — before taking a 6-5 lead and forcing it back on Osaka.

But Osaka, after throwing her racket in frustration, whipped out four straight points and a 120 mph serve that sent Zakharova backward to force another tiebreak. Her serve was suddenly back, and she easily won the tiebreak 7-3 to end things there and avoid the third set.

Osaka had 11 aces in the win, 10 of which came in the second set.

Osaka reached the semifinals last year in New York, though she fell to Amanda Anisimova in that round. She has been a threat at the previous three Grand Slams in 2026, too, and picked up career-best runs at both the French Open, where she reached the fourth round, and Wimbledon, where she reached the quarterfinals.

While she hasn't won yet this year, Osaka is fresh off a semifinal appearance at the D.C. Open and a quarterfinal run at the Canadian Open in the lead up to the US Open. Based on Monday night's outing, Osaka is in peak hard-court form. She'll take on Katerina Siniakova next in the second round.

Even though we're just getting started in New York, and it wasn't as dominant as it looked like it was going to be, Osaka is off and running at the US Open. It's a start.

articles.title: Tsitsipas no se corta sobre el positivo por cocaína de Kyrgios: "No lo voy a encubrir cuando sé la verdad"
articles.standfirst: "Cuando lo vi, fue como… más o menos lo esperaba, para ser honesto. Me sorprende que haya llegado tan tarde, eso sí"
articles.summary: "Cuando lo vi, fue como… más o menos lo esperaba, para ser honesto. Me sorprende que haya llegado tan tarde, eso sí"
articles.body: Stefanos Tsitsipas ha confesado que no le sorprendió que Nick Kyrgios fuera suspendido del tenis por consumo de drogas (dio positivo por cocaína tras un torneo en Mallorca). "Para ser sincero, era algo que cabía esperar... Aunque me sorprende que haya tardado tanto en conocerse", reconoció el jugador griego sobre el controvertido tenista australiano, que podría enfrentarse a una suspensión de cuatro años. Tsitsipas, que habló sobre el 'caso Kyrgios' tras ganar a Artur Fils en la primera ronda del US Open, confesó que "para ser totalmente sincero, yo ya estaba al tanto de esto antes del anuncio. Yo mismo lo sabía". "¿Qué puedo decirte? Simplemente te diré la verdad. Sabía todo esto antes de que se hiciera ningún anuncio y, cuando lo vi en las redes sociales, pensé: 'Aquí vamos'. Para ser sincero, me lo esperaba", insistió. Tsitsipas, que llamó "acosador" a Kyrgios tras un intenso y polémico partido en Wimbledon en 2022 (en el que el grieto la lanzó un par de pelotazos al australiano), declaró que "sabía que eran cosas que ocurrían fuera de las pistas de tenis. Eso te lo aseguro". "No voy a intentar encubrir a alguien cuando conozco la verdad. Me considero una persona amable con todo el mundo, pero se trataba de comportamientos de los que tuve noticia personalmente en el circuito; escuché a otras personas de ese mismo entorno decirme cosas por el estilo", dijo el tenista heleno. El australiano Nick Kyrgios volvió a recaer en sus demonios cuando parecía que había dejado atrás su infierno de autolesiones, pensamientos suicidas, drogas, alcohol, maltrato... Su último incidente ha sido su positivo por cocaína por el que ha sido suspendido temporalmente. "Recientemente di positivo por cocaína en un control antidopaje en Mallorca. Cometí un error grave y asumo toda la responsabilidad por ello. No voy a poner excusas, pero quiero contextualizar la situación en la que me encontraba. Los dos últimos años marcados por las lesiones han pasado una factura enorme, tanto física como mentalmente. Mi cuerpo no ha sido capaz de responder a lo que mi mente le exigía, y aceptar que me acerco al final de mi carrera ha sido más difícil de lo que jamás imaginé", reconoció el tenista australiano de 33 años en su cuenta de Instagram. Nick Kyrgios confesó en una entrevista concedida en 2022 al canal australiano 'Nine' su lucha contra sus problemas de salud mental: "El equilibrio es algo con lo que me cuesta lidiar. Siempre he sido así desde que era un niño. Los partidos siempre fueron una montaña rusa". "Realmente me esfuerzo mucho. A veces es una lucha para mí. Algunos días me despierto y vengo a las pistas o me despierto y simplemente no quiero salir de mi habitación. Lidio con problemas humanos normales, pero también estoy orgulloso de mí mismo. Salgo, mantengo la cabeza baja y juego bien. No es fácil hacerlo semana tras semana"... soy dos personas muy diferentes en la pista y fuera de ella", explicó. Nick Kyrgios no dudó a la hora de contestar a cómo de graves fueron los problemas de salud mental que sufrió en 2019: "Fueron muy serios... hasta el punto hasta llegarme a autolesionar el brazo... y eso no está bien". El intenso dolor emocional llevó a Kyrgios a "cortarme y quemarme en una mierda bastante jodida". "Sentí que estaba decepcionando a la gente todo el tiempo. Me sentí inútil y odié mi vida en un momento", reconoció. "Supongo que alejé a todos los que se preocupaban por mí y no me estaba comunicando. Simplemente me cerré la vida real y estaba tratando de manejar y abordar mis problemas de frente. Estaba abusando mucho del alcohol y las drogas, y eso se salió fuera de control", reconoció el tenista australiano. En febrero de 2020 Kyrgios ya habló sobre su grave crisis personal de 2019: "Tenía pensamientos suicidas y estaba, literalmente, sufriendo para salir de la cama y jugar para millones de personas. Estaba solo, deprimido, negativo, abusando de alcohol y drogas que me alejaron de la familia y los amigos. No podía hablar con nadie o confiar en nadie". Nick Kyrgios explica que superó esa crisis gracias a su familia y a "adoptar hábitos más saludables como la dieta, dormir bien, tratar de entrenar un poco más". "Ahora apenas bebo, literalmente tomo una copa de vino en la cena", explica Kyrgios en la entrevista. Para el tenista australiano fue "agotador" tratar con gente que "realmente no le importaba quién era yo como ser humano, sino sólo un tenista... el tenista loco" y reconoce que se ha sentido "utilizado". Kyrgios reconoce que tiene una relación de amor y odio con el tenis: "Me encanta el deporte; soy un gran estudioso del juego y a veces disfruto viendo tenis. Pero me gusta hasta cierto punto. Es mi vida y le he dedicado horas y horas que nunca voy a recuperar". Los representantes legales de Nick Kyrgios alegaron en 2022 ante un tribunal australiano que el tenista sufre problemas de salud mental con el objetivo de desestimar los cargos de maltrato presentados contra él. La agencia EFE publicó que el tenista fue acusado de un cargo de agresión común por presuntamente maltratar a Chiara Passari -su exnovia- en diciembre de 2021. Kyrgios y Passari habrían mantenido una acalorada discusión debido a una presunta infidelidad del tenista, teniendo que intervenir la policía para apaciguar la situación.

articles.title: US Open: Naomi Osaka inspired by former NBA legend Allen Iverson for night session outfit
articles.summary: Naomi Osaka made her latest fashion statement ahead of her first round match against Anastasia Zakharova at the US Open; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
The two-time US Open champion emerged from the tunnel onto the court in Arthur Ashe Stadium wearing a long, white skirt and a hooded robe featuring newspaper clippings about her.

When she removed that to reveal her black outfit, Osaka had her hair done in cornrows, just as Iverson did when was the NBA MVP while playing for the Philadelphia 76ers.

She advanced to the second round after overcoming a stern challenge from ‌Anastasia Zakharova to secure a 7-6 (8-6) 7-6 (7-3) victory.

"It's my, I guess, my tribute to Iverson. I really like him a lot," Osaka said. "I mean, Nike said basketball, so I said, 'OK, you want basketball, I'll give you basketball.'"

She wore a shirt with Iverson's picture when she met with the media on the eve of the tournament and called him a "trailblazer".

"I think he's also someone that I look up to a lot, because he's kind done a lot in fashion, whether it's on purpose or not, but he's shifted the way that NBA players dress," Osaka said Saturday.

"I also think the whole conversation around clothes in sports and also just expressing yourself through style, I feel like he's someone that I look up to in that regard."

Osaka added that they'd never communicated, but Iverson posted a message her on his Instagram page Monday, writing: "Wow, what a honor!! BIG FAN can't wait to meet you."

Swiatek swats aside Wang for a winning start at US Open

Former champion Iga Swiatek got her campaign off to a solid start as the Polish eighth ‌seed defeated China's Wang Xiyu 6-2 6-3 to reach the second ​round.

Swiatek claimed her first title of an inconsistent year in Toronto earlier this month and ​followed it up with a run to ‌the Cincinnati semi-finals, arriving in New York with a confidence boost as ​she bids for a seventh Grand Slam crown.

"For sure it was a good day in the office," Swiatek ​said on court after her 88-minute workout.

"I ⁠felt pretty good right from ⁠the beginning and I had the energy and the intensity. I want to keep ‌it that way. Wang was playing deep with lot of top-spin so I needed the strength.

"It's nice to come ‌to a Grand Slam after a couple of good results, especially because this swing is never one I've felt super comfortable at. I've made a lot of progress and ⁠I'm focused on improving the little things in ​my game."

Eighth seed Ben Shelton recovered from a shaky ‌start to beat Tallon Griekspoor 1-6 6-1 7-6 (7-3) 6-2 in the first round.

Shelton, who is looking to become the first American man ​to win the title since 2003, has endured a disappointing run in this year's Grand Slams but arrived ​in New York with momentum after successfully defending ‌his Canadian Open title earlier this month.

It was far from straightforward for the 23-year-old, ​however, as Griekspoor looked to follow up his stunning upset of top seed Alexander Zverev in Montreal.

"I started off a little bit ​nervous tonight, but I found my rhythm at some ⁠point through the second set," said ⁠Shelton, who is still hunting a first Grand Slam title.

"Obviously, a lot of credit to Tallon, ‌he's a good player to play, he doesn't give you a lot of rhythm. He has an attacking game style and I ‌found things really difficult for the first set tonight."

Wawrinka's emotional US Open finale ends in defeat

Former champion Stan Wawrinka lost to Italy's Matteo Berrettini 7-6 (7-4) 7-6 (7-3) 6-0, with the 41-year-old Swiss playing his final Grand Slam tournament before retiring at the end of the season.

"It's been 20 years since the first time I came here. It was amazing for me to feel the New York vibes throughout the years. I found the way to play my best tennis here," Wawrinka said.

Berrettini, a semi-finalist in New ​York in 2019, will face Mariano Navone in the second round after the Argentine produced the tournament's biggest upset by knocking out fourth seed Novak Djokovic in ‌five sets on Sunday.
